analysis.one_liner: Bans grossly excessive prices during emergencies and lets the FTC and states sue large price-gougers.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 17, 2025 with ten Democratic and independent cosponsors and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unlawful to charge a "grossly excessive price" for any good or service, with special rules that kick in during "exceptional market shocks" — disasters, energy shortages, public health emergencies, or sudden shifts in trade policy [S2]. Large companies (over $1 billion in U.S. revenue, or with dominant market share) would face a presumption of violation if they raised prices sharply above their pre-crisis levels or competitors' prices and could not prove the increase came from costs beyond their control [S2]. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could sue for injunctions, restitution for consumers, and civil penalties that reach up to 5 percent of a parent company's annual revenue [S2]. Publicly traded companies would also have to disclose detailed pricing and margin data to the SEC after any quarter with a market shock [S2]. The bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced, and no further action has been taken [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially during emergencies when essentials like food, fuel, and lodging spike in price. The bill gives the FTC and state attorneys general new tools to sue price-gougers, recover money for affected consumers, and hit large violators with penalties up to 5 percent of their parent company's annual U.S. revenue [S2]. Businesses with under $100 million in U.S. revenue are exempt, and any company can escape liability by proving its price increase was driven by uncontrollable costs [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers hit by emergency price spikes

how_it_helps.text: Makes selling a good or service at a "grossly excessive price" unlawful for sellers at any point in the supply chain, not just retailers at the final sale [S2].

During an exceptional market shock — a disaster, power shortage, public health emergency, or emergency declaration by the President — large sellers (at least $1 billion in U.S. revenue, a dominant market position, or a critical gatekeeping role) are presumed to violate the law if they price well above their own pre-shock average or competing sellers' prices, and must prove by clear and convincing evidence that costs beyond their control caused the increase [S2].

Gives the FTC independent power to sue for injunctions, civil penalties, and damages or restitution on behalf of aggrieved consumers; companies with unfair leverage face penalties up to 5 percent of their parent entity's annual revenue [S2].
Lets state attorneys general bring the same cases in federal or state court for their residents, and preserves all state price-gouging laws [S2].

Requires publicly traded companies to disclose, in the filing after any shock quarter, how much of their revenue growth came from higher prices versus volume, their gross margins by product line, and a narrative explaining their pricing strategy [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations — major retailers, grocers, fuel sellers, and other big sellers of essentials — would bear the cost through new litigation exposure, penalties up to 5 percent of parent-company revenue, and detailed SEC pricing disclosures after crisis quarters [S2]. The Treasury would also appropriate $1 billion for FTC enforcement [S2]. A good-faith objection supporters would have to concede: broad new price authority, enforced through an FTC-defined "grossly excessive price" standard, carries some risk of chilling legitimate price increases needed to cover real shortage costs [S2].

drawbacks.text: The FTC must define "grossly excessive price" within 180 days, with the bill suggesting a starting point of 120 percent of the prior six-month market average; critics of broad price regulation argue such standards can penalize sellers whose higher prices reflect genuine supply scarcity, potentially discouraging them from stocking goods in a crisis [S2].

Public companies face substantial new compliance costs: tabular disclosures of volumes, prices, margins, and cost changes by category, plus a narrative pricing-strategy explanation, for every quarter following a market shock [S2].
The bill appropriates $1 billion to the FTC for enforcement through fiscal 2033, a significant new federal expenditure [S2].

Because the presumption of violation applies during broadly defined market shocks (including "any other cause of an atypical disruption" and any presidential disaster declaration), the reach of the new liability would depend heavily on FTC guidance and future administrations' enforcement priorities [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is direct: a federal backstop against opportunistic pricing during the moments when people can least shop around, with money recovered through restitution and penalties scaled to company size so they actually bite. The main costs are borne by large corporations, not ordinary people, though the honest caveats are real: the FTC's discretion in defining "grossly excessive" could sweep in some legitimate cost-driven pricing, the SEC disclosures add compliance expense, and the $1 billion appropriation is a meaningful public cost. On balance, the design includes escape hatches — a small-business exemption, an affirmative defense for uncontrollable costs, and preserved state laws — that narrow the risk of overreach [S2].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any other action for the rest of the session so far.

narrative.text: Sen. Warren introduced the Price Gouging Prevention Act of 2025 in the Senate on July 17, 2025 [S1].
The bill had ten cosponsors at introduction: eight Senate Democrats and independent Sen. Sanders, with no Republican support [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history as of this analysis [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the large corporations that would face liability under the bill: with the bill stalled in committee, federal price-gouging penalties and the new pricing disclosures have not taken effect, and emergency price spikes remain governed only by the uneven patchwork of existing state laws.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations that would face liability

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's ten supporters is a Democrat or independent; no Republican senator has signed on, and the bill sits with a committee whose majority is Republican.

industries.industry: Large retailers and sellers of consumer essentials (grocers, big-box chains, fuel and lodging sellers)
industries.note: Sellers with $1 billion or more in U.S. revenue, dominant market share, or gatekeeping leverage would face a presumption of unlawful gouging during emergencies, penalties up to 5 percent of parent-company revenue, and suits by the FTC and state attorneys general. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against consumers', since the liability exists precisely to curb prices consumers pay in a crisis [S2].

Any issuer that files a 10-Q or 10-K would have to disclose detailed pricing, volume, margin, and cost data plus a narrative pricing strategy for every quarter following a market shock — a real compliance cost, though the same disclosures would give investors and the public visibility into whether revenue growth came from higher prices or more sales [S2].
Firms below the $100 million revenue threshold are exempt from the prohibition, avoiding the new litigation exposure that applies to their larger competitors [S2].
The bill hands the FTC a new enforcement mandate, rulemaking authority, independent litigation power, and a $1 billion appropriation available through fiscal 2033 [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and a Commerce Committee majority of the other party, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in this Congress unless the political environment around consumer prices changes sharply. Its most likely path is to expire in committee at the end of the session, with the possibility of reintroduction in a future Congress.
